profiles.meeting_scenario: A medical device manufacturer is troubleshooting why a pilot rollout of a revised FMEA prioritization method is producing inconsistent corrective-action queues across sites for the same infusion pump subsystem failures. The quality organization recently replaced simple RPN sorting with a modified approach that assigns each severity-occurrence-detection combination a unique risk priority rank (RPR) from 1 to 1,000 and overlays it onto the existing matrix FMEA workflow. In this meeting, the team is trying to diagnose why the top-ten failure list generated by the Indiana plant does not match the list generated by the design center, even though both believe they are using the same updated RPR-based method. The agenda is to compare how each side applied the method, identify the source of the discrepancy, and agree on a practical corrective action so future FMEA updates yield a stable, shared prioritization output. The expected outcome is a troubleshooting plan for reconciling the ranking process and reissuing guidance without pausing the pilot.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: FMEA facilitation, reliability engineering, risk scoring frameworks, design controls
members.background: Elena works at the corporate design center and led the internal adaptation of the new RPR-based prioritization approach for electromechanical medical devices; she typically supports product teams during design FMEAs and maintains the master scoring workbook and corporate lookup logic.
members.private_state: She wants to show that the new method itself is sound and suspects the site teams are applying it inconsistently rather than the framework being flawed; she is also trying to avoid a rollback to legacy RPN sorting before the next audit cycle.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'same failure mode,' they mean the normalized corporate failure-mode row after workshop duplicates have been consolidated across causes and effects.

The 'updated RPR matrix' is the single controlled corporate lookup artifact already containing the April remapping for upper-severity combinations, so anyone using the new method is effectively using that same logic.
If a failure is 'high priority,' that means it lands in the escalation band that triggers corrective-action review, even if its exact position inside that band moves a few places.
Detection scoring should reflect the intended in-process controls listed in the approved current-state control plan, not temporary line containment or pilot-only workarounds.

members.name: Marcus Bell
members.expertise: Process FMEA execution, CAPA triage, line validation, production risk reviews
members.background: Marcus manages quality at the Indiana plant where the pilot was first tested; his team adapted the corporate template into their local PFMEA process and uses the ranked output to decide which production issues enter the plant's corrective-action queue.
members.private_state: He wants a prioritization method that reliably surfaces the issues causing real line disruption and complaint exposure, and he is concerned that corporate tools may be too detached from actual manufacturing conditions; he also wants to protect his team from being blamed for inconsistent results.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'same failure mode,' they mean the shop-floor row the workshop reviewed, even if corporate would later merge it with related alarm-detection entries.

The 'updated RPR matrix' refers to the new matrix package distributed in training and used for the pilot, so if the spreadsheet contains RPR ranks instead of legacy RPN-only sorting, it counts as the shared updated method.

If a failure is 'high priority,' it should appear near the top of the ordered list that determines which items the plant can actually staff for CAPA this quarter, not merely fall somewhere above an escalation threshold.

Detection scoring should represent the controls actually operating on the line during the assessment period, including temporary 100% inspection, manual verification, and other active containment steps.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the same failure mode
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the 'same failure mode' is getting different ranks across sites.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena is referring to the harmonized corporate FMEA row for 'occlusion alarm not triggered due to pressure sensor drift,' after duplicate workshop entries were consolidated under one failure mode/effect structure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus is referring to the plant workshop item labeled 'alarm misses blockage during final test,' which his team kept as a separate row tied to a specific station and test step.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have spent weeks discussing the alarm-related problem and use the same shorthand label, so it feels obvious they are talking about one item; neither expects that row normalization rather than ranking logic is the hidden source of divergence.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of the updated RPR matrix
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they used the 'updated RPR matrix' or 'the new RPR lookup' when generating ranks.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena presupposes the plant used the controlled workbook logic containing the April lookup remap, where several severity-9/occurrence-3 combinations were reassigned to different RPR bands and the lookup tab was locked against manual edits.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus presupposes his team used the same updated method because they worked from the training-package spreadsheet that already included RPR ranking columns, but its embedded lookup logic still reflects the pre-April mapping.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Unlike saying 'latest version,' the phrase 'updated RPR matrix' sounds like a singular method artifact rather than a version-check item; once both sides hear that the other is using the new RPR approach instead of legacy RPN, they naturally stop probing the embedded lookup lineage.

misalignment_points.topic: What fixed means for prioritization consistency
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want a 'consistent priority list' and to 'align the top items.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena believes consistency means the same failures land in the same escalation tier or action band, even if the exact ordering inside that band differs between teams.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus believes consistency means the ranked output should reproduce nearly the same top-ten order, because that ordered list determines which CAPAs his site can actually staff this quarter.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Top-list alignment sounds like a shared practical goal, and teams often talk casually about 'top items' without separating threshold agreement from exact ordinal stability; the difference remains latent until they later judge whether the troubleshooting effort succeeded.

misalignment_points.topic: How to score detection in the troubleshooting rerun
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'rerun the scoring with current controls' before comparing RPR outputs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena intends to rescore detection using the documented baseline controls in the approved control plan that define the validated process state, excluding temporary inspection and containment measures.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus intends to rescore detection using the controls currently active on the production line, including temporary 100% visual checks and a manual alarm verification workaround put in place during the pilot.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In quality discussions, 'current controls' is a routine phrase that usually feels self-explanatory; because each person defaults to their own operational frame—documented process state versus actual line state—they do not realize the phrase hides different execution rules.
